title: The Farmer Who Invented Chinese Paper Money
event_summary: In 1024, the Song Dynasty government officially took over the issuance of 'jiaozi' — the world's first government-backed paper currency — after decades of private banknotes had circulated among Sichuan merchants and tea farmers. The system originated around 1000 AD when a group of sixteen wealthy merchants and farmers in Chengdu, frustrated by the impossibility of hauling thousands of pounds of iron coinage across mountain trade routes, began issuing standardized promissory notes backed by their pooled deposits. When several private issuers defaulted, the Song court under Emperor Renzong nationalized the system, establishing a dedicated Bureau of Exchange to print, regulate, and periodically retire the notes — creating the template for every central bank that would follow.
why_forgotten: The Mongol conquest and subsequent dynasties disrupted institutional memory, and catastrophic hyperinflation under the later Yuan Dynasty made paper money a cautionary tale rather than a celebrated invention. Western financial histories long credited European banking houses with pioneering modern monetary instruments, marginalizing Chinese precedents. The merchants who originated the system left almost no personal records, making them invisible beside emperors and generals.
why_it_matters: Every modern economy runs on fiat currency — money backed by government authority rather than intrinsic metal value — and this concept was born in a Sichuan marketplace six centuries before European banknotes appeared. The Song Bureau of Exchange was functionally the world's first central bank, establishing principles of money supply management, note expiration, and anti-counterfeiting measures that the Federal Reserve and European Central Bank still employ. The lesson of its eventual collapse through overprinting also remains the foundational warning in modern monetary policy.
